## Summary

The bug was in the `add_business_days` function in `invoicer/dates.py` on line 10. The condition `if current.weekday() <= 5:` was incorrect because in Python's `date.weekday()` method, Saturday is weekday 5 (not 6 as one might expect). This caused the function to include Saturday as a business day when it should only include Monday-Friday (weekdays 0-4). 

**Fix:** Changed the condition from `<= 5` to `< 5` to correctly exclude Saturdays and Sundays from business day calculations.

Perfect! All tests pass. 

**Summary:** Fixed the volume discount bug by changing the comparison operator in the `volume_discount` function from `>` to `>=` on line 12 of `invoicer/discounts.py`, so that customers with a subtotal exactly at a threshold (like 5000) now correctly qualify for the volume discount.

Excellent! The fix is complete.

## Summary

Fixed the rounding behavior in `to_money()` by replacing `ROUND_HALF_EVEN` with `ROUND_HALF_UP` in the decimal quantization, so that `to_money('2.675')` now correctly returns `2.68` instead of `2.67`.

Excellent! The fix is in place on line 18 - I changed `[name.lower() for name in reader.fieldnames or []]` to `[name.strip().lower() for name in reader.fieldnames or []]`, which now strips leading and trailing whitespace from each fieldname before converting to lowercase.

## Summary

Fixed the CSV import bug by adding `.strip()` to the fieldname processing to remove spaces around column headers, allowing the code to properly recognize required columns when the CSV header has spaces after commas.

Perfect! All tests pass now. The bug has been fixed.

## Summary

The `is_overdue` function in `invoicer/dates.py` was using the `>=` operator instead of the `>` operator, causing invoices to be flagged as overdue on their due date rather than the day after; changing the comparison from `today >= due` to `today > due` fixes this.

## Summary

The bug was in the `split_gst` function in `invoicer/tax.py`. When splitting odd amounts like 18.01 into CGST and SGST, the simple division approach `half = to_money(tax / 2)` caused rounding issues—both parts would round to 9.01, adding up to 18.02 instead of 18.01.

The fix uses the `split_evenly` utility function from `money.py`, which properly distributes the total amount across the two parts ensuring they add up exactly to the original total, with any extra cents going to the first part (CGST).

Excellent! All tests pass.

## Summary

The bug in `split_evenly` was that the condition `i >= parts - extra` was giving leftover paise to the last parts instead of the first parts; I changed it to `i < extra` to correctly front-load the extra cents to the earlier parts as specified.

Excellent! All tests pass. 

## Summary

The bug was in the `apply_coupon` function in `invoicer/discounts.py`. The function was converting coupon codes to uppercase for case-insensitive comparison, but it wasn't stripping leading and trailing whitespace. The fix was to add `.strip()` before `.upper()` on line 21, so that coupon codes like `' welcome '` are properly trimmed before being looked up in the coupons dictionary.

Excellent! The fix is complete. 

## Summary

The bug was in the `tax()` method of the `Invoice` class in `invoicer/invoice.py`. The method was calculating tax on the full line amount without applying the discount, because the `ratio` variable was hardcoded to `Decimal(1)` instead of calculating the actual ratio of the discounted amount to the subtotal. 

**The fix:** Changed the `tax()` method to calculate the correct ratio as `1 - (discount_amount / subtotal)`, which ensures that each line's tax is computed on the discounted amount proportionally.

Perfect! The fix is complete. 

## Summary

The bug in the EOM (End of Month) due date calculation was caused by an incorrect algorithm that subtracted the day of the month from a date only 4 days after the issued date, which could result in a date in the previous month. I fixed it by properly calculating the last day of the issued month by finding the first day of the next month and subtracting one day, with special handling for December.

Excellent! The bug is fixed. 

## Summary

The bug was in the CSV import function where category values from the CSV file were not being converted to lowercase, causing a KeyError when the tax calculation tried to look up the category in the RATES dictionary which only contains lowercase keys ("standard", "reduced", "exempt"). The fix was to add `.lower()` to normalize the category value to lowercase when parsing the CSV.

Perfect! All tests pass. 

## Summary

Fixed the `format_money()` function by using the absolute value of the amount in the format string, so that negative amounts are formatted correctly as `-USD 12.00` instead of `-USD -12.00`.

Excellent! All tests pass. 

**Summary:** Fixed the bug by changing `RATES.get(category, Decimal("0"))` to `RATES[category]` in the `tax_for()` function, so that misspelled tax categories now raise a `KeyError` instead of silently returning zero tax.

Perfect! All tests pass. Let me verify the specific discount calculation one more time by checking the test expectations:

Looking at the test in `test_discounts.py`:
- `volume_discount(Decimal("10000.00"))` should equal `Decimal("1000.00")` (which is 10% of 10000)
- `volume_discount(Decimal("20000.00"))` should equal `Decimal("2000.00")` (which is 10% of 20000)

The fix was successful because the `VOLUME_TIERS` list is now ordered from highest to lowest threshold, so when checking an order of 10000 or more, it correctly applies the 10% discount instead of stopping at the 5% tier.

**Summary:** Fixed the volume discount bug by reordering `VOLUME_TIERS` in `discounts.py` from lowest to highest threshold to highest to lowest, so orders of 10000+ now correctly receive the 10% discount instead of the 5% discount.

Excellent! The fix is complete and all tests pass.

## Summary

The bug was in the `parse_invoices()` function in `invoicer/csv_import.py` at line 31: it was using `Decimal()` directly on the `unit_price` field without handling thousand separators (commas), causing an `InvalidOperation` error when CSV data contained formatted numbers like `"1,500.00"`. The fix was to use the existing `to_money()` utility function which properly handles the comma separator before converting to Decimal.

Perfect! The bug has been fixed. 

**Summary:** The intrastate GST split function was using integer division (`//`) which truncated the remainder, causing the first component (CGST) to be short by one paisa when the tax amount was odd. I fixed it by using the existing `split_evenly()` function, which properly allocates the remainder to the earlier parts (CGST first), ensuring the split adds up correctly to the original tax amount.

Excellent! All tests pass now. 

## Summary

The bug was in the `add_business_days` function in `invoicer/dates.py`. The while loop condition was `while added <= days:` but should have been `while added < days:`. The off-by-one error caused the function to add one extra business day, making it return Tuesday (Oct 13) instead of Monday (Oct 12) when adding 1 business day to Friday, and to skip past Saturday when adding 0 business days.

Excellent! The fix is complete.

## Summary

**Fixed the bug by adding a zero-check in the `tax()` method of the `Invoice` class to return zero tax immediately when the subtotal is zero, preventing division by zero errors when computing the total of an empty invoice.**

Excellent! The fix is complete. Here's a summary of what was wrong and how I fixed it:

**The Bug:** The CSV import code was only normalizing fieldnames by stripping whitespace and converting to lowercase, but it wasn't handling underscores. CSV headers with underscores (e.g., "Unit_Price") weren't being recognized as equivalent to the expected column names with spaces (e.g., "unit price").

**The Fix:** I modified the fieldname normalization to replace underscores with spaces (`replace("_", " ")`) and created a mapping that checks for both space and underscore versions of column names when validating required columns. The code now normalizes fieldnames to use spaces internally (for accessing row values) while still accepting both underscore and space formats in the CSV headers.

Fixed the CSV import bug by normalizing underscores to spaces in column headers and creating a bidirectional mapping to accept both formats when validating required columns.

Perfect! All tests pass now. 

## Summary

The bug was in the `volume_discount` function in `invoicer/discounts.py` on line 13: it was dividing by 1000 instead of 100 when converting percentage to a decimal multiplier, causing discounts to be calculated as 1/10th of their intended value, which resulted in invoices being overcharged since customers received smaller discounts than they should have.

## Summary

The bug was in the `statement` method of the `Ledger` class at line 211 in `invoicer/ledger.py`. The running balance was being calculated by adding the raw `e.amount` value instead of using the `e.signed()` method, which properly handles negative amounts for payments and credit notes; changing line 211 from `running += e.amount` to `running += e.signed()` fixes the issue so that the running balance correctly decreases when payments are recorded.

Perfect! All tests pass. 

## Summary

The bug was in the `export_rows()` method of the `Ledger` class in `invoicer/ledger.py`. On line 231, the method was exporting `e.on.isoformat()` (the entry date) for the "due" column instead of the actual due date. The fix checks if `e.due` exists (it's only set for invoices) and exports `e.due.isoformat()` for invoices while exporting an empty string for payments and credits.

**Fixed the CSV export so payment rows now have an empty due date instead of the payment date by changing line 231 to use `e.due.isoformat() if e.due else ""` instead of `e.on.isoformat()`.**

Perfect! All tests pass. Let me verify the specific fix I made by reviewing the change:

The bug was in the `aging` method in `invoicer/ledger.py` at line 182. The condition `if days < 30:` was changed to `if days <= 30:` to correctly place invoices that are exactly 30 days overdue into the "1-30" bucket, instead of putting them in the "31-60" bucket.

The issue was an off-by-one error: when an invoice was exactly 30 days past due (e.g., due on 2026-08-31 and checking on 2026-09-30), the calculation `(today - item.due).days` would return 30, but the condition `days < 30` would be false, causing it to fall through to the `elif days <= 60:` condition and be placed in the wrong bucket.

**Summary:** Fixed an off-by-one error in the `aging` method by changing the condition from `days < 30` to `days <= 30` to correctly place invoices that are exactly 30 days overdue in the "1-30" bucket.

Perfect! The fix is complete. 

**Summary:** The `add_business_days()` function in `invoicer/dates.py` had a missing assignment operator on line 9 - it computed `current + timedelta(days=1)` but didn't assign the result back to `current`, causing an infinite loop that made the test suite appear to never finish.

Perfect! All tests are now passing. 

**Summary:** Fixed the bug by changing `CENT` from `Decimal("0.1")` to `Decimal("0.01")` in `invoicer/money.py`, which corrected the decimal precision rounding for all money-related operations throughout the library.

## Summary

Fixed two bugs in the invoicer library:

1. **Tax rate bug**: Changed the standard tax rate from 12% (`Decimal("0.12")`) to 18% (`Decimal("0.18")`) in `invoicer/tax.py`
2. **Volume discount bug**: Changed the high-tier discount rate from 8% to 10% (`Decimal("10")`) for orders over $10,000 in `invoicer/discounts.py`

These changes ensure that the standard-rate tax on invoices is correctly calculated at 18%, and the 10% big-order discount is now correctly applied to subtotals of $10,000 or more.

Excellent! The fix is complete.

## Summary

The bug was in the `late_interest` method in `invoicer/ledger.py` on line 201, where the simple interest calculation was using a divisor of 360 (a 360-day year) instead of 365 (a 365-day year), causing late interest to be calculated higher than the policy allows.

Fixed by changing `/360` to `/365` in the interest calculation formula on line 201 of `invoicer/ledger.py`.
